ESSENCE: [0] Śṛṅgāra is performed, not described: the separated beloved's voice, her appeal to the cloud, and the landscape's answering her are all determinants (vibhāva) of the rasa. The cloud is never told to carry a message — that is dhvani, and it is what makes it the genre's first instance. The voice closes not in despair but in sustaining memory: the sthāyibhāva (love) transforms the sorrow (vyabhicāri) into something relishable. Kāma arises in the heart to kill; the beloved who is absent arises with him; the cātaka, thirsty for rain alone, begs water; the peacock-flock sounds at the clouds; she is protected only by remembrance of his virtue.

No new doctrines, no comparisons, no meta-commentary, no quoted terms. ESSENCE: [0] Beauty is not decoration but cause: the groves shine for Kāma's sake, not the reverse. The grove is the vibhāva (determinant) of śṛṅgāra; the rasa overwhelms perception — dust of passion obscures sun and moon, new-cloud-drunk peacocks cry. The kuṭaja's mockery and the nīpa's release are consequents (anubhāva), not ornament: the poet sides with the humble tree over showy flowers. The bee kisses the yūthikā creeper. The rasa is aesthetic: the rasa IS the point.

items.prompt: Render the argument of this song in a Gen-Z voice: direct, a little feral, zero cringe, no slang overload. Keep every doctrinal claim intact — voice changes, content does not. No new doctrines, no comparisons, no meta-commentary, no quoted terms. ESSENCE: [0] The rasa shifts from śṛṅgāra to vira/adbhuta: love and landscape are framed by the poet's skill, not by love alone. Clouds thundering make travelers long; sorrow grows, endless. Lovers honor the love-festival; cloud-arrival, dear friend, they bring. Then the tribute: may I be conquered by which poet, by yamakas; to him I pour water in ghaṭakarpara. The sthāyibhāva (love) resolves into the poet's own delight (camatkāra) at his craft. The potsherd is both vessel and namesake — the potsherd names itself at its close.
